title: THE ADDRESS IS NOT THE IDENTITY
subtitle: UNTIL THE REST OF THE INTERNET CONNECTS THE DOTS.

blocks.text: A CRYPTO ADDRESS DOES NOT CONTAIN YOUR NAME. THAT DOES NOT MAKE IT ANONYMOUS.
THE ADDRESS

Imagine generating a new Bitcoin address. Nobody has used it before. Nobody has publicly connected it to you. Someone looking at the blockchain sees an address and nothing more. They do not automatically know who controls it.
That part is real. Public blockchains generally expose transactions without embedding a person's legal identity directly into the address itself. The mistake is assuming the story ends there.
IT IS NOT ANONYMOUS. IT IS PSEUDONYMOUS.
THEN YOU USE IT

You receive funds. You send funds. You interact with other addresses. Perhaps several addresses are eventually used together. Perhaps you reuse an address. Perhaps funds move to or from an exchange. The ledger starts accumulating history.
Your address still does not print your name beside the transaction. It does not have to. The transaction graph is building context.
THE GRAPH COMES FIRST

On Bitcoin-style UTXO networks, one established technique is the common-input ownership heuristic. If several addresses are spent together as inputs to one ordinary transaction, analysts may have evidence that the keys were controlled together. Those addresses can begin forming a cluster.

These techniques are not infallible. Collaborative transactions such as CoinJoin can break simplistic assumptions, and responsible analysis has to account for those failure modes. The graph is evidence and inference, not omniscience.
NOBODY NEEDED YOUR NAME YET. THEY STARTED BY MAPPING YOUR BEHAVIOR.
THEN THE GRAPH TOUCHES REAL LIFE

Eventually, one piece of the puzzle may encounter something that knows who you are. A regulated exchange is an obvious example. You created an account. You verified your identity. You deposited or withdrew crypto. Now identity data and blockchain data can intersect.
The blockchain did not suddenly discover your identity. Something outside the blockchain supplied context. That distinction matters.
ATTRIBUTION

First came clustering: which addresses appear to belong together? Then comes attribution: who or what is behind them? Attribution can incorporate information outside the blockchain, including interactions with known services, public information and other evidence.

One sufficiently strong attribution can potentially give meaning to a larger cluster of previously pseudonymous activity. That is why saying 'my name is not on the blockchain' misses the point. It does not necessarily need to be.
YOU CAN IDENTIFY YOURSELF

Sometimes nobody needs sophisticated analytics at all. Post a donation address publicly. Associate an address with an online identity. Reuse an address people already know belongs to you. Move funds between known services and your wallet. Every public connection can become another piece of context.
The clue you reveal today can give meaning to transactions that happened years earlier. The graph was already there. The label arrived later.
THIS DOES NOT MEAN EVERY ADDRESS CAN BE IDENTIFIED

Blockchain analysis is not magic. An address cannot always be reliably attributed to a specific human. Heuristics have limitations. Clustering can be wrong. Different wallet architectures behave differently. Off-chain evidence varies enormously in quality.
THE LESSON IS NOT THAT EVERY ADDRESS HAS YOUR NAME ATTACHED TO IT.
PSEUDONYMOUS IS NOT ANONYMOUS

A pseudonym protects you while the connection between the pseudonym and your identity remains unknown. But a public financial graph does not disappear when that connection is discovered. Your transactions can exist first. Your identity can arrive later. Once those datasets meet, history can become much easier to interpret.
SOURCES // VERIFY IT YOURSELF
THE ADDRESS WAS NEVER THE IDENTITY.
IT WAS THE THREAD LEADING TO IT.
